title: Design a Text Editor
statement:
Build a class `TextEditor` that holds a line of text and a cursor. The cursor sits between two characters or at either end, and it can never leave the text: its position is always between `0` and the text's length.

- `TextEditor()` starts with empty text and the cursor at position `0`.
- `addText(text)` inserts `text` at the cursor and leaves the cursor just after the inserted characters.
- `deleteText(k)` erases up to `k` characters immediately to the left of the cursor, like pressing backspace `k` times, and returns how many characters were really erased (fewer than `k` when fewer are available).
- `cursorLeft(k)` moves the cursor `k` positions to the left, stopping at the start of the text.
- `cursorRight(k)` moves the cursor `k` positions to the right, stopping at the end of the text.

After moving, `cursorLeft` and `cursorRight` both return the characters directly to the left of the cursor, at most the last `10` of them (all of them when there are fewer than 10, or `""` when there are none).
constraints: text consists of lowercase English letters
At most 2 * 10^4 calls in total are made to addText, deleteText, cursorLeft and cursorRight
notes:
## Intuition

Keeping the text as one string with a cursor index is easy, but every insert or delete in the middle copies the whole string. The edits only ever happen right next to the cursor, so split the text at the cursor into two stacks: `left` holds the characters before the cursor (its top is the character just left of the cursor), and `right` holds the characters after it in reverse (its top is the character just right of the cursor). Typing, backspace and cursor moves then only touch the tops of the stacks.

## Approach

1. `addText`: push each character `ch` of `text` onto `left`; the cursor ends after them automatically.
2. `deleteText`: `removed` is the smaller of `k` and the size of `left`; pop that many and return `removed`.
3. `cursorLeft`: move up to `k` characters from the top of `left` to the top of `right`, stopping when `left` is empty.
4. `cursorRight`: move up to `k` characters from `right` back to `left`, stopping when `right` is empty.
5. Both moves return the last 10 entries of `left` joined into a string.

## Example 1, step by step

`addText("leetcode")` makes `left = leetcode`. `deleteText(4)` pops 4 characters and returns `4`, leaving `leet`. `addText("practice")` gives `left = leetpractice`. `cursorRight(3)` finds `right` empty, so nothing moves, and the last 10 characters of `left` are `"etpractice"`. `cursorLeft(8)` moves `ecitcarp` onto `right`, leaving `left = leet` and returning `"leet"`. `deleteText(10)` can only remove 4 and returns `4`. `cursorLeft(2)` has nothing to move and returns `""`. `cursorRight(6)` pops `p, r, a, c, t, i` back onto `left` and returns `"practi"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(text.length) for `addText` and O(k) for the other calls, plus O(10) to build each returned string.
- Space: O(total characters typed) across the two stacks.

## Pitfalls

- `deleteText` returns how many characters were really erased, not `k`.
- Stop moving when a stack runs empty: the cursor cannot go past either end of the text.
- `right` is stored reversed, so pop from its end to get the character nearest the cursor.
- Build the returned string after the move, and from at most the last 10 characters of `left`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `left` | characters before the cursor, nearest one on top |
| `right` | characters after the cursor, reversed so the nearest one is on top |
| `ch` | a character being typed |
| `removed` | how many characters `deleteText` really erases |
| `i` | how many positions have been processed so far in a loop |
